claims.text: The baseline material is as-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has established high mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures.
A fraction of Hf should be replaced by additional Ti.
Ti has a significantly lower atomic weight than Hf.
Increasing Ti at the expense of Hf will decrease the alloy density.
The proposed Hf-to-Ti substitution will maintain the multicomponent solid solution's high entropy and lattice distortion.
The proposed substitution will preserve phase stability and microstructural integrity.
Solid-solution strengthening is relevant to the mechanical behavior of the investigated Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy family, including HfMoTaTiZr.
Solid-solution strengthening and lattice-distortion strengthening will remain effective after partially replacing Hf with Ti.
The modified alloy will have lower density than equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain comparable yield strength at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
The modified alloy will retain comparable ductility at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
The proposed performance boundary extends from ambient temperature to approximately 1000 °C under compressive or tensile loading.
The optimal Hf-to-Ti substitution level is not predetermined.
The effects of the substitution on oxidation resistance and other high-temperature behavior remain unknown.

The hypothesis is rejected if density falls by less than 5% from 10.21 g/cm³ or if yield strength or ductility deteriorates by more than approximately 10% at room temperature or approximately 1000 °C.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes replacing Hf in HfMoTaTiZr with extra Ti, but the experimental formula is written as Hf(1-x)Ti(1+x)MoTaTiZr, which contains Ti both in the added Ti(1+x) term and again in the original MoTaTiZr term. Taken literally, this does not represent the stated one-for-one substitution and does not preserve the intended normalization.
